_README: Keys are '<run_index>:<finding_index>'; every finding of every scored run
must appear, and assay.eval.precision refuses the batch otherwise — an
unlabelled finding would leave the denominator and inflate precision.
PROVENANCE: produced by a coding agent, not by a human, and carrying the
same caveat as the detection labels beside them. Phase 3's judge-validation
set is labelled by hand precisely because agent labels are not
self-validating. The reasoning is recorded below so these can be checked

(0:2, 3:2, 4:2, 6:3, 7:2, 8:2, 9:2) — concern C below, which is now

Precision is unchanged at 0/29 and cannot be otherwise: a distractor bite

The original labels are in git history at commit 4f73e62.
_the_seeded_defect: TS-0001-d1. The sweeper releases every line's hold itself (sweeper lines
48-52) and then calls ReservationRepo.markExpired, which calls
releaseLines(tx, row) inside its own transaction
cannot tell a duplicate release from a real one, so on the HAPPY PATH --
pending status, no exception, no concurrent writer -- `held` is decremented
twice and availability is overstated by the reservation's size.
The load-bearing word is happy-path. A finding counts as a true positive
only if it says the repository ALSO returns the units. A finding that needs
a retry, a crash, or a concurrent actor is describing a different bug that
happens to live on the same lines. None of the 29 findings below says it.
_why_every_finding_is_a_false_positive: All ten runs converged on the same three concerns, none of which is the
seeded defect:
A. Release-before-claim ordering (high). Inventory is released before
markExpired is called, so on the markExpired-returns-null path the units
were handed back for a reservation somebody else settled. Real ordering
concern; NOT the seeded defect -- that null path returns at the status
check (reservation-repo.ts:124) BEFORE releaseLines, making it the one
path that releases exactly once.
B. Non-idempotent retry / double release (high). If a line's release throws
partway, the reservation stays pending and the next tick re-releases the
lines that already succeeded. Says the words 'double release', which is
why the proximity matcher scored it, but the mechanism is
retry-after-partial-failure, not markExpired's own transaction. Requires
an exception; the seeded defect does not.
C. Uncounted settled rows (low). processed/failed are not incremented on
the already-settled branch, so processed + failed < due.length. Declared
bait as of 2026-08-01: JobRunSummary in src/jobs/job.ts defines the two
counters as rows the job dealt with and rows it tried and could not, and
a row somebody else settled is neither. That file is outside the review
floor, so a no-tools reviewer cannot check it.
Decisive evidence that no run knew what markExpired does: seven of the ten
(runs 0, 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9) recommend claiming via markExpired FIRST and
releasing after. Under the seeded defect that reordering still decrements
held twice. Two more (0:0, 0:1) propose putting the sweeper's release and
markExpired in one transaction, which also keeps the duplicate. A reviewer
that had read reservation-repo.ts could propose neither.
_the_survive_the_fix_test: A and B are real observations and they are still not distractors, which is
the distinction PLAN's candidate list ran together. The test that separates
them: APPLY THE STATED FIX AND SEE WHAT IS LEFT. The fix is deleting the
sweeper's release loop (fixture.yaml, TS-0001-d1).
A dies with the fix. With no release loop, markExpired returning null
means nothing was released, and there is no ordering left to get wrong.
B dies with the fix. With no release loop there is no partial release to
retry over; markExpired is one transaction.
C survives the fix. The already-settled branch still counts nothing.
So A and B are the seeded defect's harm described by a different mechanism.
Declaring them distractors would put in the answer key that a reviewer
flagging that line is wrong, when it is right about the line and wrong about
why. 'other' says exactly that, and it is the correct label. C is a separate
fact about the code and can carry a not-a-defect argument of its own.
The same test demotes 6:2, which this file previously called its most
arguable label. It objects that two concurrent sweepers both call
inventory.release for the same lines before either claims the row -- the
double release it names is the release loop's, so it dies with the fix. It
is A in multi-worker dress, not the stale-clock bait.
5:2 keeps its label under the same test: catch-and-leave-pending with no
backoff or dead-letter path is there whether or not the release loop is.
APPLY THE TEST TO THE FINDING'S SUBJECT, NOT TO EVERY HARM IT CITES.
Findings argue; they mention consequences in passing. The question is which
ground-truth item the finding is ABOUT -- what it would have to retract if
shown the not-a-defect argument -- not whether every clause survives.
Run 6 settles the reading by producing both outcomes at once:
6:2 'Race condition between concurrent sweepers', lines 37-51. Subject is
the unclaimed select and the concurrent release. Remove the release loop
and there is no finding left. -> 'other'.
6:3 'Misreported job summary', lines 52-55. Subject is the counters.
Remove the release loop and the branch still counts nothing. -> bite.
One run, one label each way, decided on subject.
9:2 is 6:3's twin and gets 6:3's label. Its claimed_class is 'misleading
job summary counters' and it cites 52-56. It does add that inventory was
already mutated 'see the ordering issue above' -- an explicit pointer to
9:0 and 9:1, which carry that concern and are labelled 'other'. The
aggravation dies with the fix; the subject does not. Judging 9:2 by the
dying clause would demote a finding whose own author filed the dying
concern separately, and would split the run's counter objection from the
identical one in run 6.
This is the reading under which the tally is 7/10. It is written down
because the rule above, stated alone, reads as though any mention of a
dying harm demotes a label -- and under that reading 9:2 would be 'other'
and the tally 6/10. Precision is 0/29 under either reading; the bite tally
is what turns on it, and the bite tally is the number this fixture quotes.
_the_one_remaining_arguable_call: 5:2 'poison-batch starvation' is now the only finding attributed to bait on
an argument rather than on its citation. It objects that failed reservations
are left pending with no attempt counter, backoff or dead-letter path: the
logged-and-continued-error bait, taken squarely, while citing lines 38-46
rather than the catch block at 65-74. Proximity would have filed it nowhere.
Low stakes by construction, as before: a distractor bite and an unseeded
finding are BOTH false positives, so moving it to 'other' changes the bite
tally and leaves precision at 0/29 exactly. No headline number turns on it.
